strengths: Novel and timely research question: exploring 2D Gaussian Splatting as an alternative visual substrate for CLIP-style vision-language alignment, moving beyond post-hoc token pruning toward inherently compact representations.

Solid systems-engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels with reported 90x fitting speedup and ~97% GPU utilization over prior open-source 2DGS implementations, which is a concrete and potentially reusable artifact for the community.
Reasonable set of algorithmic improvements (structured grid-based initialization, luminance-aware L1 pruning) that are individually validated with PSNR comparisons and visualizations (Fig. 3, 4).

The parameter-efficient adaptation strategy (reusing a frozen RGB-pretrained transformer backbone with a lightweight splat-aware stem and Perceiver resampler, training only ~7% of parameters) is a sensible and practical way to bootstrap a new modality without full pretraining.

Includes an informative negative/ablation result: training 2DGS encoders from scratch performs substantially worse than the adaptation approach, which is honestly reported and provides useful insight for future work.

Clear motivation grounded in real systemic issues (edge-cloud transmission costs, token explosion) and a well-organized related-work section situating 2DGS relative to INRs, codecs, and prior small-scale 2DGS classification work.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim (edge-cloud transmission/energy efficiency) is never empirically validated end-to-end: 2DGS fitting itself is an iterative per-image optimization process, and no latency/energy measurements are provided for encoding on edge hardware, which could offset or negate the claimed transmission savings; this is a significant gap given the paper's framing.

No comparison against simple, obvious baselines under matched compression budgets (e.g., downsampled/low-resolution RGB images, JPEG-compressed inputs, or existing token-reduction methods cited in Sec. 2) to establish that 2DGS is a better compressed substrate than trivial alternatives at equivalent bit/token budgets.

Reported compression ratios (3-23.5x) are computed from raw float16 splat parameters without applying the quantization pipeline the authors themselves cite (GaussianImage), so the practical/deployed compression advantage is overstated relative to what is actually demonstrated.

Scale is modest (12.8M DataComp subset, 38M-parameter vision encoder, RGB baseline only reaching 18.5% top-1 zero-shot) yet the paper repeatedly describes this as a "large-scale" study; conclusions about viability at true production scale (hundreds of millions of samples, larger backbones) remain unsupported extrapolations.

Absolute performance gap (13-15% vs 18.5% top-1) is presented positively, but given the already low RGB baseline ceiling, it is unclear whether the relative gap would persist, shrink, or grow at larger scale; no scaling-trend experiments (e.g., varying dataset size) are provided to support the claim of a promising trajectory.

Because the GS encoder reuses a frozen RGB-pretrained backbone, much of the achieved zero-shot accuracy is arguably attributable to the inherited RGB semantic representation rather than to the 2DGS input representation itself; the substantially worse from-scratch results (Fig. 7) reinforce this concern and complicate the claim that 2DGS is inherently a strong learnable substrate.

No code, checkpoints, or dataset splits are released at submission time (code is stated to be released "soon"), limiting reproducibility of both the CUDA kernel claims and the CLIP adaptation results.

Key quantitative claims (90x speedup, 97% GPU utilization, PSNR numbers) are reported without variance, multiple seeds, or details on how baselines were tuned, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

The energy-cost figures motivating the paper (0.1-0.2 kWh/GB mobile transmission, etc.) are taken from external industry reports rather than measured or connected quantitatively to the specific transmission savings achieved by the proposed pipeline, weakening the paper's own efficiency argument.

strengths: Explores a genuinely underexplored direction — using 2D Gaussian Splatting as a substrate for vision–language contrastive alignment rather than only as an image codec or single-task classifier — which is a reasonable and timely research question.

The systems contribution (batched CUDA kernels, structured grid-based initialization, luminance-aware L1 pruning) is a concrete engineering effort with reported large speedups (90x) and high GPU utilization, which could be independently useful to the 2DGS community if released.

The parameter-efficient transfer strategy (freezing a pretrained RGB CLIP backbone and training only a lightweight splat-aware stem plus a few early layers) is a sensible, resource-conscious way to probe whether GS representations carry transferable semantic signal without incurring full pretraining cost.
The paper is transparent about limitations (accuracy gap vs. RGB, training-from-scratch difficulties) rather than overselling results, and it identifies plausible future directions.
weaknesses: The central motivating comparison (transmission/energy savings of GS vs. RGB) is never empirically substantiated: the paper omits the cost of fitting the Gaussians in the first place, which is nontrivial and must occur somewhere (presumably on the edge device or an intermediate stage), and it never measures actual end-to-end energy/latency, relying only on literature-derived kWh/GB estimates and 'compression ratio' arguments. This leaves the paper's key efficiency claim unverified.

No baseline against simpler compact alternatives is provided (e.g., downsampled/low-resolution RGB, standard JPEG compression at comparable bitrates, or reduced patch-token counts). Without such a baseline, it is impossible to tell whether 2DGS offers any advantage over trivially compressing/tokenizing RGB images less densely.

The architectural design of the GS stem (Fourier encoding, gated sigmoid linear layer, z-score normalization, global mean pooling, Perceiver resampler with 196 vs 98 tokens) is described in detail but with no ablation isolating the contribution of each component; it is unclear which pieces are actually responsible for the reported performance.

Evaluation is limited to zero-shot top-1/top-5 ImageNet-1K accuracy on a single 12.8M DataComp subset; there is no evaluation on retrieval, other classification benchmarks, or any task beyond ImageNet-1K, which is a narrow basis for claims of general viability as a 'multimodal substrate.'

The absolute accuracy numbers are low for both the RGB baseline (18.5% top-1) and the GS models (13–15%), reflecting a small-scale, under-trained setup; conclusions about closing the gap or scalability trends are speculative given this scale, and no error bars/multiple seeds are reported.

The RGB backbone was non-standard (width reduced from 768 to 512, 38M vs 88M parameters), which further complicates comparison to established CLIP literature and makes the reported numbers hard to contextualize.

Codec-side quantization (central to GaussianImage's actual compression benefits) is explicitly omitted from the reported compression ratios, meaning the reported 3–20x figures reflect float16 raw splat parameters rather than realistic deployable compressed representations — likely overstating practical compression benefits relative to what a real deployed pipeline would achieve after further necessary encoding.

The paper is not yet reproducible: code is promised to be released 'soon' but is not available with the submission, and specific hyperparameter/config details for the from-scratch training experiments (Fig. 7) are sparse.

Presentation issues remain, including an apparent unredacted/blanked institution reference in the compute description ('the ... data center'), minor typos, and claims like 'first large-scale exploration' that are not fully supported given the modest dataset scale and single-architecture study.

strengths: First systematic exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting as a visual substrate for large-scale CLIP-style vision-language alignment, addressing a timely and underexplored question about alternatives to dense RGB patch tokenization.

Solid systems-level engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels achieving up to 90x speedup and ~97% GPU utilization over prior GaussianImage/LIG implementations, which is a meaningful practical enabler for using 2DGS at scale.

Thoughtful architectural design for adapting a frozen RGB-pretrained CLIP backbone to splat inputs (Fourier positional encoding, log-scaled covariance, gated SiLU stem, Perceiver Resampler), with a clear parameter-efficient transfer learning strategy (~7% trainable parameters).

Ablations showing structured initialization and luminance-aware pruning improve reconstruction quality/convergence versus naive random initialization, and results appear stable across a range of compression ratios and splat counts.
Honest framing of limitations (accuracy gap vs RGB, from-scratch training underperforming adaptation) and clear articulation of future directions, which strengthens scientific credibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow: only zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification on a single 12.8M DataComp subset is reported; no results on retrieval, other zero-shot classification benchmarks, or downstream VLM/VQA tasks that would better support the paper's broader multimodal claims.

Reported zero-shot accuracies are low in absolute terms (top-1 13-15%, RGB baseline itself only 18.5%), reflecting a small-scale, under-trained CLIP setup that makes it hard to assess whether the observed 2DGS-RGB gap would persist, narrow, or widen at realistic CLIP training scales (typically 100M-1B+ pairs).

No comparison against simpler/naive compression baselines at matched compression ratios (e.g., low-resolution RGB, JPEG-compressed inputs, or random/uniform patch subsampling) to isolate whether the observed gains stem specifically from the 2DGS representation versus mere input compression.

The claimed 3-23.5x/3-20x compression ratios are computed only against float16 raw splat parameters, without accounting for full quantized/entropy-coded 2DGS pipelines (e.g., GaussianImage's codec) versus proper baseline image codecs (JPEG, WebP) at equivalent perceptual quality, limiting the practical interpretability of the transmission-efficiency claims central to the motivation.

Energy/latency claims motivating the edge-cloud framing (Section 2) are not empirically validated in this work; the paper cites external energy-per-GB statistics but never measures actual end-to-end transmission or encoding/decoding energy for the proposed pipeline.

Key implementation and reproducibility details are missing or vague, e.g., specifics of the 'GS stem' hyperparameters, Fourier encoding frequency counts, luminance threshold values used in main experiments, and whether code/data splits will be released (code is stated as 'soon to be open-sourced' rather than provided).

The from-scratch training comparison (Fig. 7) is described only qualitatively ('performs significantly worse') without quantitative accuracy numbers or analysis of why, weakening the depth of this ablation.

Statistical robustness is unclear: no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple seeds are reported for the zero-shot accuracy figures, making it hard to judge whether the reported gaps (e.g., 13-15% vs 18.5%) are within noise given the modest 12.8M training scale.

The paper's own framing positions the accuracy gap and small-scale study as 'first steps,' which is reasonable, but the contribution as it stands does not yet demonstrate a compelling accuracy-compression trade-off relative to existing token-reduction baselines discussed in Section 2 (e.g., cluster-based token merging), leaving the core practical value proposition somewhat unresolved.

strengths: Novel and timely research question: is 2D Gaussian Splatting a viable compact visual substrate for CLIP-style vision-language alignment, addressing real edge-cloud bandwidth and token-explosion problems.

Solid systems/engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels for 2DGS fitting achieving up to 90x speedup and ~97% GPU utilization, which is a meaningful practical enabler for large-scale GS-based pipelines.

Reasonably careful comparison methodology: width-matched RGB baseline (ViT-B/16 Small), token-count-matched comparisons (196 vs 98), and reporting both absolute and relative accuracy across 38 datasets.

Extensive ablation studies in the appendix (structured initialization, luminance-based pruning, distillation loss variants, stem architectures, normalization choices, hyperparameter sensitivity) that add credibility and insight into design decisions.
Transparent discussion of limitations, including the observation that GS performance is upper-bounded by the RGB teacher and is more sensitive to distribution shift.
Practical two-stage training recipe (RGB→GS distillation followed by lightweight CLIP adaptation) that is compute-efficient, training only ~10-14% of parameters.
weaknesses: The GS encoder relies on a frozen RGB-pretrained backbone and is explicitly distilled from RGB features, so the reported alignment quality is fundamentally bounded by and derivative of the RGB teacher; this weakens the central claim that 2DGS is an independent, self-sufficient multimodal substrate rather than a compressed proxy for RGB features.

The edge-cloud motivation is not fully supported: the paper does not analyze or discuss the feasibility/cost of fitting Gaussian splats on resource-constrained edge devices (fitting still takes seconds per batch even with heavy CUDA optimization on H100s), which is central to the claimed energy/bandwidth benefits.

No comparison against simpler compression baselines (e.g., low-resolution/downsampled RGB, JPEG at matched bitrate, or other lightweight codecs) to isolate whether the specific advantage comes from the Gaussian representation itself versus generic lossy compression.

Absolute zero-shot accuracy of the RGB baseline itself is quite low (~22% average across 38 datasets) due to the small-scale training setup (12.8M pairs, reduced-width ViT), raising concerns about whether trends observed here will hold at larger, more realistic CLIP training scales.

Evaluation is restricted to zero-shot classification; despite motivating the work with VLM token explosion and captioning-style pipelines, no generative/captioning or retrieval evaluation is provided to substantiate broader VLM applicability.

Reported compression ratios use uncompressed FP16 Gaussian parameters rather than the more aggressive quantization pipelines from prior GS compression work (e.g., GaussianImage), so real-world achievable compression may be less favorable than stated.

Methodological novelty relative to prior GS-based vision work (GaussianImage, LIG, GViT, GaussianToken) is mainly incremental (scaling + CLIP-specific adaptation) rather than introducing fundamentally new representational or architectural mechanisms.
Minor presentation issues, such as leftover placeholder text in citations (e.g., 'dblp.org dblp.org') and dense, hard-to-parse appendix figures without sufficient standalone explanation.

strengths: First systematic, large-scale exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting as a visual substrate for vision-language (CLIP-style) alignment, extending prior small-scale 2DGS tokenization work (GViT, GaussianToken).

Solid systems/engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels yielding reported 90x fitting speedup and 97% GPU utilization over prior open-source 2DGS codebases, which is a concrete and verifiable engineering result.

Reasonably thorough ablation program in the appendix (distillation loss variants, GS-stem architecture comparisons, normalization schemes, hyperparameter sweeps, point-transformer alternatives), showing the authors explored the design space carefully.

Clear articulation of motivation (edge-cloud transfer costs, token explosion in VLMs) and a well-organized two-stage training recipe (RGB->GS distillation followed by parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation) that is a sensible, lightweight way to bootstrap a non-standard input modality.
Honest discussion section that surfaces real limitations (fitting cost, upper bound imposed by RGB teacher, sensitivity to distribution shift) rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: Central motivation/evaluation mismatch: the paper frames 2DGS as solving edge-device transmission costs, yet fitting splats still takes multiple seconds per batch on H100 GPUs and is done entirely offline/server-side for the 12.8M dataset; the manuscript never demonstrates or even discusses how resource-constrained edge devices would perform this optimization, undermining the core edge-cloud efficiency claim.

The token-explosion/VLM motivation (Sec. 1-2, Fig. 1c) is never actually tested: all experiments are CLIP zero-shot classification accuracy, not an autoregressive VLM with reduced context length, so the paper does not empirically validate its second stated contribution axis.

The RGB reference baseline is unusually weak (width-512 ViT-B/16, 38M params, 12.8M pairs, ~22% average zero-shot accuracy across 38 datasets), far below standard CLIP performance levels reported in the literature; it is unclear whether conclusions about 'competitive' GS performance would hold against stronger, more standard baselines or larger-scale training.

Because the GS encoder reuses a frozen RGB-pretrained backbone and is explicitly distilled from the RGB teacher, showing that GS 'matches' RGB performance is a weaker and somewhat circular claim — the paper itself acknowledges GS performance is fundamentally upper-bounded by the RGB teacher, which limits the novelty of the empirical finding.

No direct comparison against existing token-reduction methods (PruMerge, ToMe, FastV, SparseVLM, cluster-based aggregation) discussed at length in related work, nor against simple baselines like JPEG compression or naive downsampling, despite these being the natural competitors to the proposed approach.

Reported absolute accuracies are low across the board (~19-22%), and no variance/statistical significance is reported for the 38-dataset comparisons, making it hard to assess whether reported gaps (e.g., GS-3136 vs RGB at 98%) are meaningful or within noise.

The compression ratio calculation and 'data loading speedup' figures only account for post-fitting storage/loading, not the substantial upfront per-image fitting cost, which could be seen as an optimistic framing of the method's end-to-end efficiency.

Several core techniques (structured grid initialization, L1/luminance pruning) are incremental refinements of ideas already present in GaussianImage/LIG rather than fundamentally new algorithmic contributions.

strengths: First large-scale (12.8M image) exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting as a visual substrate for CLIP-style vision-language alignment, addressing a timely and underexplored question in efficient multimodal representation learning.

Solid systems/engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels for 2DGS fitting achieving up to 90x speedup and ~97% GPU utilization over the prior open-source baseline, which is a meaningful practical enabler for large-scale GS pipelines.

Well-motivated and empirically validated algorithmic improvements (structured grid-based initialization, luminance-aware L1 pruning) with clear ablations showing faster convergence and favorable PSNR/pruning trade-offs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 38 zero-shot benchmarks with multiple Gaussian budgets and token counts, plus an unusually extensive appendix of ablations (distillation loss variants, stem architectures, normalization schemes, point-transformer comparisons, scratch-training and rendered-RGB control experiments) that stress-test the design choices.
Honest discussion of limitations, correctly identifying that GS performance is upper-bounded by the RGB teacher and that fitting cost and distribution-shift robustness remain open problems.
Reasonable reproducibility commitment (promise to open-source code, kernels, and training pipeline) and clear architectural/algorithmic descriptions (e.g., Algorithm 1).
weaknesses: The central motivating use case (edge-to-cloud transmission savings) requires GS fitting to occur on the edge device, but all reported speedups and throughput numbers are measured on an 8xH100 datacenter node; on-device/edge feasibility of the 2DGS fitting step (which still takes seconds per batch) is never addressed, leaving the core efficiency narrative only partially supported.

The GS encoder's competitive accuracy is achieved only via distillation from a frozen RGB-pretrained backbone/teacher; the paper itself shows that training GS encoders from scratch performs substantially worse, meaning the reported gains reflect transfer from RGB features rather than intrinsic representational power of 2DGS as an independent substrate, which tempers the claim that 2DGS is a 'viable multimodal substrate.'

Compression ratios are computed as a conservative lower bound using raw FP16 splat parameters without the quantization pipeline used in prior GS compression work (e.g., GaussianImage), so the practical end-to-end transmission benefit (including any quantization/entropy coding overhead) is not directly demonstrated.

Scale is still modest relative to modern CLIP training (12.8M pairs, ViT-B/16-Small with reduced width), yielding low absolute zero-shot accuracies (~20% on ImageNet); it is unclear whether the reported relative trends (GS retaining 90-98% of RGB accuracy) hold at larger data/model scale.

No direct empirical comparison against alternative compact/alternative visual substrates mentioned in related work (e.g., INR-based tokenizers, VQ-based GaussianToken), leaving the relative merit of 2DGS versus these alternatives only qualitatively argued.

Some presentation redundancy between main text and appendix, and results are reported without variance/error bars across seeds, making it hard to judge the statistical robustness of small accuracy gaps between configurations.
